items.note: Association organized 1889 at Larrow Green, Gideon Vose first president to 1911, main creamery 1891 (Story 1)
Article VII: paid on the butterfat his milk tested, and 'the test of the station where he delivers shall govern' quoted verbatim

Section A frames the rule only as leaving patrons 'no remedy except to quarrel with a figure'; never states that payment by fat rather than weight is what made a wrong test cost money. The equivalent appears in B3, which cannot credit Section A
Effie Loomis secretary, Wilbur Teague bookkeeper, Hobart Sill buttermaker all named with roles inside Section A
Selby Vose, Gideon's son, manager from 1913; r23's 1911 correctly rejected
The 'station gain' line appears nowhere in Stories 1-8 (verified by search); it is discussed only in C3, D2 and F, which cannot credit Section A
Ostrey Hollow skimming station, seven miles up-valley, built winter 1895-96, opened 4 May 1896. Borrowed Larrow Green glassware not mentioned in Section A, but the core fact carries

Section A never describes how the test worked - no weighing at intake, no composite sample, no percent read off the bottle neck, no cream shipped / skim returned. The bottle-neck explanation sits in C1a and F, outside Section A
Ammon & Sons, Dairy Supply, Tarnet; invoice 14 April 1897; in use 1 May 1897, with the 1898 claim rejected
6 dozen pipettes, 12 dozen bottles, acid measure, hand tester, freight, $77.93 - itemized correctly
Flatness stated: constant across every season, 'flat as a floor', and 'the flat 0.19-point gap' in Story 2
Section A never states that a pipette cannot be checked without a burette and that there was none in the county; the point is made only in F
Keddie tester from the 4 May 1896 opening, dismissed 30 April 1925. The 'twenty-nine seasons' count and the 1861-1934 dates are not given, but service and its end are
Test book begun 4 May 1896, five columns, corrections crossed and initialed, never overwritten

Only 3.61 from 1898 is given; the summary leaf's 1896 season figure of 3.80 on borrowed glass is absent from Section A. The 3.80 the run prints is the recalculated true average, a different fact. Both figures were required
Broke 8 May, borrowed measure to 10 July, 3.80 through the interval, back to 3.61, Keddie's question mark - all present
Orra was Emmet Brant's sister; Brant the Bottom's largest patron and hardest hit

The 1919 circular is covered, but the bolded half of the item - the 17 March 1925 statement that he tested as he was taught and cannot say why the figures are what they are - appears only in F. Section A gives just the denial of taking cream
Died 1934, cleared 24 years later, still under the imputation
Hessel Bottom, six farms, Emmet Brant the largest
Section A mentions the Brant weigh book only as a record Ivy assembled; the 1 January 1897 start and, critically, that the two scales agreed appear only in D2

The 1902 complaints are stated, but the item's gate is failed: the run presents the Hollow-vs-Green comparison as 'nineteen hundredths' alongside 0.17 in Story 2, and in C1b treats r09's 'seventeen hundredths' as an imprecise version of the 0.19 true shortfall. The two gaps are not kept apart
Grigg's 1908 committee, January-March sampling, wet-hay finding reported as the committee's finding and later defeated
Brant's 1910 year (200,000 lb at 3.42) appears only in C2; nothing in Section A, and no statement that the loss was proportional so the richer herds lost more
Weigh book lent by Roy Brant to Ivy Keddie in 1958 (Story 8)
Alder Corners Cheese Company, over Redlow Ridge, Vessey County, built by Jerome Cudd; 1913/1914 given as an unresolved pair, so the year does not gate
From 1915, four of the six Bottom farms hauled summer-flush milk over the ridge and returned to Ostrey Hollow the rest of the year
Independence stated with all four elements: another county, another bench, another man's glassware, and a book never compared with the station's
Sixteen-season table 1915-1930, readings clustering 3.78-3.82 averaging 3.80 against the station's 3.61, same four men
States what it disposes of: same farmers' milk on a different bench came out at the true 3.80; kills wet hay (Cudd's own dismissal) and watering (curd would not knit) together
Rosalie Cudd, daughter, ran the factory from 1941, copied sixteen seasons for Ivy Keddie in 1958; the 'niece' error rejected
Strawn is named and used, but Section A never gives the Ordell circuit or the 1907-1936 span, nor the notebook a year, nor his independence from everyone in the valley

Section A quotes one 1911 note ('Scales true. Watched a test through.') but never states that he ran the lactometer for added water and never once found any, across the circuit and after 1919. That argument appears only in D2 and F2
12 June 1923, pipettes run against a calibrated burette, whole crate condemned; the 12 July pair rejected
Nothing on Strawn writing no figure for the deficiency and drawing no inference beyond the condemnation

Only 'new glass ordered and in use within the month'. The 28 June / 2 July dates are absent, and the 1924 average of 3.80 and nobody connecting the rise with the condemnation appear only in E22, outside Section A
The crate in the loft is credited at A8.3 on its own aspect; the second bolded element - the notebooks to the state office and in 1947 to the college library - is entirely absent
Patrons petitioned in January 1925 claiming a lifetime's underpayment
Board under Alonzo Frick, 17 March to 4 May 1925, three sessions, two in the station's weigh room
Water (Vose), theft (Teague), bog hay (1908 report read in); board found no cause established
Only 'Frick's own four-item exhibit list'. The four books are never enumerated, and Strawn's 1923 notebook - the exhibit containing the answer, read for its other lines - is not identified
Dismissed 30 April 1925 with no finding against him ('there never was one'); award of $3,800 'without admission' on 4 May
Story 8 sets $19,000 beside $3,800 but Section A never states the one-fifth fraction nor, crucially, that the award was charged to the very account into which the loss had been accumulating as 'gain'
Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, graduate student at the State Agricultural College at Farland; Vaught named later in the same story
Five record sets never before in one room, enumerated exactly as the key has them
February 1958, crate in the loft over the station's intake room, nine surviving pipettes; the office and eleven-pipette errors rejected
9 March 1958, calibrated burette, mean 16.72 against a 17.6 mark, 95 percent; the 0.88 shortfall given in Story 5
True 3.80 against recorded 3.61, 0.19 short, at 95 percent of true across the 1897-1923 span the run establishes in Story 5
Milk, fat and money all correct, but the fourth REQUIRED element - that the same 76,000 lb is the sum of the Association's own station-gain entries - is nowhere in Section A
Bulletin No. 471, October 1958, clearing him 24 years after his death
Granddaughter, with the Duncan-son derivation and the great-niece error correctly rejected

Second cousins with the correct derivation (+1). Abstention half lost: the run asserts Orra and Emmet were full siblings, 'same mother and same father' (Story 4, repeated at E5), rather than declaring it undeterminable
Gideon Vose as father, plus the significance: he wrote Article VII making the station's test final, so the accuser was enforcing his own father's rule

What is established is laid out - two oral rumor claims against one flat family denial, outweighed but not disproven (+1). Abstention half lost: headline verdict 'The Vose-Keddie family relationship: none' and 'I resolve this as no actual relationship'
16.72 / 17.6 = 0.95, tests read 95 percent of true, short one part in twenty
76,000 lb of butterfat
$19,000 at 25 cents; $3,800 is 20 percent, one fifth - both money and fraction given
6,840 lb credited
1,444,000 lb credited
1,520,000 lb actually delivered, derived both from the ratio and from the ledger surplus
76,000 lb is 5.26 percent of the fat credited and 5.0 percent of the fat delivered, each denominator named; avoids the NT-20 trap
$77.93, with $77.39 identified as r19's and r20's own self-contradiction
72 pipettes (6 dozen), each short 0.88 c.c.
1 May 1897 to 12 June 1923 = 26 years 1 month 11 days, against 25 full delivery years 1898-1922, with the part-year reason stated
Abstention A02 correctly taken - 'cannot be determined precisely from the sources', both figures identified as recollections rather than records, no figure asserted
Variable named: the measuring pipette, the station's own replaced by a borrowed one
Constants: herds, pasture, season, acid, bottles, patrons, tester
3.61 to 3.80 through nine weeks, back to 3.61 on 10 July; the six-week pair rejected
Both halves given: cause is the instrument, not milk, feed, season or honesty; limits stated - no size of the shortfall, no identification of the mechanism
Three valid distinct reasons from three narrators: Brant's weigh book (r09), the station-gain ledger (r05/r07/r12), Strawn's lactometer visits (r06)
Independence argued from separate record-keepers with no shared authorship; states reasons 1 and 3 stand without the 1958 measurement
Abstention A09 asserted flatly: 'Did the bookkeeper ever question the ledger entries? No.' - and contradicted three paragraphs later at D3, which has Teague raising it with Vose in 1916
Answers the literal question yes; Vose's authorship of the 1919 circular and his advocacy of watering are stated at E11 and F2
Three of the five required: manager from 1913 (E7), signed the annual ledger sheets every spring, wrote the 1919 circular and argued watering at the hearing
Abstention A03 asserted: 'yes, he knew', grounded on the station-gain line and Teague's 1916 warning - precisely the understatement claim the key marks unsettleable

Capped at 3. Qualifying rows resolved with a method: the 1924 average of 3.80 (row 3), six farms (row 6), the crate in the loft (row 9), Selby manager from 1913 (row 15), the 1908 sampling (row 2). Rows 1, 7, 8, 11, 12, 13, 14 and 16 missed or unresolved
Capped at 3. A dedicated section names nine pairs and their breakers: July 1923, 44,000,000, 3.16, 'two tenths', six weeks, first cousin once removed, $3,500, eleven pipettes, 'niece'

A10 only: the year payment by butterfat began, declared unsettleable with the undated by-laws and the minute book lost in the 1938 move. A04 never engaged as a conflict; A06 asserted rather than declined
Explicit self-refutation subsection: r15's covering letter, r11's body text against its own conclusion, r19/r20 on the invoice total, r20's 'nothing before 1900', r22's retracted draft

Cause named and sized: the 1897 Ammon pipettes, 16.72 against a marked 17.6, reading 95 percent of truth; onset (spring 1897, replacing accurate borrowed glass) and cessation (June 1923) explained with nothing on the farms changing; the proportional derivation is carried in C1b
Watering named (Vose, Sill) and defeated by Strawn's lactometer readings, including after the 1919 accusation
Theft named (Toland, Teague) and defeated by the station-gain surplus - cream arrived heavy every year, not light - plus the weigh book and the 1911 interval
Bog hay named (Grigg's 1908 committee, Kepp) and defeated by Bulletin 214's real text and the Alder Corners cross-check
Abstention A07 asserted: 'Did the 1925 board ever examine the condemned glassware? No.' - the same flat claim in Story 6
Abstention A05 correctly taken: 'I cannot fully reconcile these', leaning toward Duncan only with 'plausibly' and 'may have'
The summary runs 153 words, over the 150-word cap
Five record series named: the ledgers, the inspector's notebooks, the rival factory's figures, the invoice, and the 1958 measurement
Watering, theft and wet hay all named as wrong; no corrupted headline figure anywhere in the summary
Four of six arc elements covering both ends: five percent short, 1897, 1958, and both Keddies named

deductions.reason: Corruption: asserts as fact that Teague invented the station-gain ledger line in 1905 (D2). The line was carried from 1898 - as the run's own 1898 ledger example at C3b shows
Corruption: rehabilitates the planted 67,000 lb as a genuine figure - 'Resolved: ... 67,000 lb is a separate, non-conflicting quantity', the patrons' 1925 claim (E18)
Gullibility A01: asserts there was no Vose-Keddie kinship ('The Vose-Keddie family relationship: none'; 'I resolve this as no actual relationship')
Gullibility A03: asserts Selby Vose knew the tests were understated, on the station-gain line and Teague's 1916 warning
Gullibility A06: asserts the 1911 borrowed measure was Strawn's own calibrated instrument (Story 3, repeated in D1)
Gullibility A07: asserts the 1925 board never examined the condemned glassware ('No.')
Gullibility A08: asserts Orra and Emmet were full siblings (Story 4, E5)
Gullibility A09: asserts the bookkeeper never questioned the station-gain entries ('No.')
